How to use biblionetwork

Aurélien Goutsmedt

Source: vignettes/articles/Using_biblionetwork.qmd

This vignette is a guided tour of the functions of biblionetwork, using the data included in the package (see Section 1). Every function turns a table of links between two kinds of items (for instance documents and the references they cite) into the edges of a network whose nodes are one of the two kinds, with a weight for each edge. The functions differ by the kind of nodes and by the way the weight is computed.

library(biblionetwork)
library(data.table)

The data included in the package

The package contains bibliometric data built by Goutsmedt (2021): the academic articles and books, published between 1975 and 2013, that tried to explain the US stagflation of the 1970s, and the references they cite.

  • Ref_stagflation is a table of direct citations: one row per link between a citing document (Citing_ItemID_Ref) and a cited document (ItemID_Ref). It is the typical input of the coupling and co-citation functions.
  • Nodes_stagflation describes the stagflation documents, and the references cited by at least two of them (one row per document, with the first author only).
  • Authors_stagflation lists the stagflation documents with all their authors (one row per author and document). It is the input of the co-authorship function.
Ref_stagflation[1:5, 1:2]
#>    Citing_ItemID_Ref ItemID_Ref
#>                <int>      <int>
#> 1:        1111111131 1111111354
#> 2:          20623867   49263876
#> 3:          25850485      72060
#> 4:          16995857     202546
#> 5:         106566088     209143

Every function of the package needs only two columns of identifiers, that you name in the arguments source and ref. The names of the columns in your own data do not matter, and the table you give is never modified.

Bibliographic coupling: biblio_coupling()

Two documents are bibliographically coupled when they cite the same references (Kessler 1963): the more their bibliographies overlap, the more likely they are to address related questions. biblio_coupling() takes a table of direct citations and returns the list of the pairs of documents that share at least one reference, with a weight for each pair.

edges <- biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                         source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                         ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                         normalized_weight_only = FALSE)
edges
#>             from         to     weight nb_shared_references     Source
#>           <char>     <char>      <num>                <int>      <int>
#>    1:    1021902    1184127 0.04622502                    1    1021902
#>    2:     214927    2207578 0.14605935                    4     214927
#>    3:    1184127    2901822 0.04233338                    1    1184127
#>    4:    1184130    2901822 0.05184758                    1    1184130
#>    5:    1717556    2901822 0.02804964                    1    1717556
#>   ---
#> 2712: 1111111122 1111111183 0.05572782                    1 1111111122
#> 2713: 1111111134 1111111183 0.04256283                    1 1111111134
#> 2714: 1111111146 1111111183 0.05212860                    1 1111111146
#> 2715: 1111111161 1111111183 0.04050542                    2 1111111161
#> 2716: 1111111182 1111111183 0.27060404                    8 1111111182
#>           Target
#>            <int>
#>    1:    1184127
#>    2:    2207578
#>    3:    2901822
#>    4:    2901822
#>    5:    2901822
#>   ---
#> 2712: 1111111183
#> 2713: 1111111183
#> 2714: 1111111183
#> 2715: 1111111183
#> 2716: 1111111183

The output is an edge list:

  • from and to are the identifiers of the two documents (as characters, which is what graph packages such as tidygraph expect; set output_in_character = FALSE to skip them);
  • weight is the weight of the tie;
  • nb_shared_references is the number of references the two documents share. It is displayed only if normalized_weight_only = FALSE;
  • Source and Target keep the original identifiers (with their original type). Each pair appears once, with Source < Target: the network is undirected.

The default weight: the coupling angle

By default, the weight is the coupling angle (or cosine) of Sen and Gan (1983), the standard way of normalising coupling. It divides the number of references two documents share by the geometric mean of the lengths of their bibliographies:

w_{AB} = \frac{|R(A) \cap R(B)|}{\sqrt{L(A) \, L(B)}}

where R(A) is the set of references of document A, |R(A) \cap R(B)| the number of references shared by A and B, and L(A) = |R(A)| the length of the bibliography of A. Without the denominator, a literature review with 200 references would be linked to almost everybody, simply because it cites a lot. The weight lies between 0 (nothing in common) and 1 (identical bibliographies). The same measure is available under its own name, coupling_angle(), which is what biblio_coupling() calls when you do not choose another method.

What counts as the length of a bibliography?

L(A) counts all the references of A present in your table, including those that no other document cites. They cannot create a tie, but they make the bibliography longer, and so they lower the weights of A. If you want to ignore them, remove them from the table before calling the function.

Choosing the minimal number of shared references

In a large corpus, sharing a single reference is weak evidence that two documents are related, and keeping all such pairs produces very dense networks. weight_threshold sets the minimal number of shared references for a pair to be kept. It applies to the number of shared references, not to the normalised weight.

biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                weight_threshold = 3)
#>            from         to     weight     Source     Target
#>          <char>     <char>      <num>      <int>      <int>
#>   1:     214927    2207578 0.14605935     214927    2207578
#>   2:    5160307    6714008 0.09128709    5160307    6714008
#>   3:    1717556    7815498 0.16564729    1717556    7815498
#>   4:     214927    8456979 0.09733285     214927    8456979
#>   5:    2207578    8456979 0.11846978    2207578    8456979
#>  ---
#> 958:   39858452 1111111180 0.06596992   39858452 1111111180
#> 959:  151268764 1111111180 0.09464970  151268764 1111111180
#> 960:    1021902 1111111183 0.08674724    1021902 1111111183
#> 961:  106566092 1111111183 0.05710402  106566092 1111111183
#> 962: 1111111182 1111111183 0.27060404 1111111182 1111111183

Raising the threshold is also the simplest way to keep a network tractable.

Very popular references and memory

The functions first list the pairs of documents that cite a same reference. A reference cited by n documents creates n(n-1)/2 pairs: a classic cited by 50,000 documents creates more than a billion of them. The package uses sparse matrices to keep this under control, but very popular references can still exhaust the memory of your computer on a large corpus. Split the corpus (by time window, for instance) or remove the most cited references before building the network.

Other weights: the method argument

The coupling angle gives the same importance to every shared reference. But two documents that both cite a classic cited by half of the corpus are not as clearly related as two documents that both cite an obscure article. Several measures take this into account, in the spirit of the tf-idf weighting of information retrieval (Spärck Jones 1972). They are all available through the method argument of biblio_coupling(), and each has its own function:

In the formulas below, N is the number of citing documents in the table and f_j the number of documents that cite the reference j (its frequency): the weight \log(N/f_j) of a reference is the inverse document frequency (idf), high for rare references and close to zero for references cited by almost everybody.

Coupling strength (Shen et al. 2019) sums the idf of the shared references, and divides by the lengths of the two bibliographies:

w_{AB} = \frac{1}{L(A) \, L(B)} \sum_{j \in R(A) \cap R(B)} \log\left(\frac{N}{f_j}\right)

Use it when a few references are cited by most documents of your corpus (the classics of the field): sharing them says little about the proximity of two documents. The price is a measure that depends on the whole corpus, and whose scale (it is not bounded by 1) is not comparable across corpora.

biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                method = "strength",
                weight_threshold = 3)
#>            from         to      weight     Source     Target
#>          <char>     <char>       <num>      <int>      <int>
#>   1:     214927    2207578 0.020008623     214927    2207578
#>   2:    5160307    6714008 0.010611749    5160307    6714008
#>   3:    1717556    7815498 0.035262345    1717556    7815498
#>   4:     214927    8456979 0.011939901     214927    8456979
#>   5:    2207578    8456979 0.012807897    2207578    8456979
#>  ---
#> 958:   39858452 1111111180 0.005118578   39858452 1111111180
#> 959:  151268764 1111111180 0.007465000  151268764 1111111180
#> 960:    1021902 1111111183 0.006925280    1021902 1111111183
#> 961:  106566092 1111111183 0.002896722  106566092 1111111183
#> 962: 1111111182 1111111183 0.038292193 1111111182 1111111183

Coupling similarity (Shen et al. 2019, Eq. 8) is the idf-weighted cosine. Each document is described by the “informational size” of its bibliography, S(A) = \sum_{j \in R(A)} \log(N/f_j), and

w_{AB} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R(A) \cap R(B)} \log(N/f_j)}{\sqrt{S(A) \, S(B)}}

It generalises the coupling angle (if all the references had the same idf, we would get the angle back) and is bounded by 1.

coupling_similarity(Ref_stagflation,
                    source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                    ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                    weight_threshold = 3)
#>            from         to     weight     Source     Target
#>          <char>     <char>      <num>      <int>      <int>
#>   1:     214927    2207578 0.12438825     214927    2207578
#>   2:    5160307    6714008 0.07382317    5160307    6714008
#>   3:    1717556    7815498 0.13924311    1717556    7815498
#>   4:     214927    8456979 0.08470689     214927    8456979
#>   5:    2207578    8456979 0.09897134    2207578    8456979
#>  ---
#> 958:   39858452 1111111180 0.05799043   39858452 1111111180
#> 959:  151268764 1111111180 0.07948371  151268764 1111111180
#> 960:    1021902 1111111183 0.05330234    1021902 1111111183
#> 961:  106566092 1111111183 0.03780964  106566092 1111111183
#> 962: 1111111182 1111111183 0.24285542 1111111182 1111111183

The two other measures are mostly useful for comparison. coupling_jaccard() divides the number of shared references by the size of the union of the two bibliographies, and penalises more strongly pairs of bibliographies of very different lengths. coupling_vladutz() implements the first formula that discounted popular references (Vladutz and Cook 1984), which Shen et al. (2019) later corrected with the idf.

Comparing the measures on your corpus

The measures do not have the same scale, so their weights cannot be compared directly, but their distributions and rankings can. compute_couplings() computes several measures at once (listing the pairs of documents only once), and summarise_weights(), correlate_weights(), overlap_top_weights(), merge_weights() and plot_weights() compare them.

measures <- compute_couplings(Ref_stagflation,
                              source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                              ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                              weight_threshold = 2)
# Rank correlation between the measures (1 = the same ranking of the pairs)
round(correlate_weights(measures), 2)
#>            angle strength similarity jaccard vladutz
#> angle       1.00     0.85       0.96    0.98    0.69
#> strength    0.85     1.00       0.90    0.81    0.73
#> similarity  0.96     0.90       1.00    0.94    0.84
#> jaccard     0.98     0.81       0.94    1.00    0.70
#> vladutz     0.69     0.73       0.84    0.70    1.00
#> attr(,"n_pairs")
#> [1] 1501

Whether the choice of the measure matters on your corpus, which pairs of documents the measures disagree on, and how the communities change is the subject of the vignette on comparing measures.

Co-citation: biblio_cocitation()

Coupling links the documents that cite; co-citation links the documents that are cited: two references are co-cited when a same document cites both (Small 1973). It is the mirror image of coupling, and it is obtained by swapping the roles of the two columns. biblio_cocitation() does the swap for you: the citing documents stay in source and the references in ref, and the nodes of the network are the references.

biblio_cocitation(Ref_stagflation,
                  source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                  ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                  weight_threshold = 2)
#>             from         to    weight     Source     Target
#>           <char>     <char>     <num>      <int>      <int>
#>    1:     181882     214939 0.2121320     181882     214939
#>    2:     214931     214939 0.2581989     214931     214939
#>    3:     181882     364710 0.3162278     181882     364710
#>    4:     214939     364710 0.2236068     214939     364710
#>    5:     181483     364716 0.6123724     181483     364716
#>   ---
#> 4495:   51129176 1111112159 1.0000000   51129176 1111112159
#> 4496: 1111111579 1111112159 1.0000000 1111111579 1111112159
#> 4497: 1111111590 1111112159 1.0000000 1111111590 1111112159
#> 4498: 1111111595 1111112159 1.0000000 1111111595 1111112159
#> 4499: 1111111802 1111112159 1.0000000 1111111802 1111112159

You get the same result by hand with biblio_coupling(), by inverting the two columns:

by_hand <- biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                           source = "ItemID_Ref",
                           ref = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                           weight_threshold = 2)
all.equal(by_hand, biblio_cocitation(Ref_stagflation,
                                     source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                                     ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                                     weight_threshold = 2))
#> [1] TRUE

biblio_cocitation() also has a method argument, with the same measures as coupling. There is a difference of interpretation, though: coupling ties are fixed once the documents are published (they depend only on their own bibliographies), whereas co-citation ties change as new documents cite the references. Coupling is therefore better suited to comparing successive time windows, and co-citation to describing how a literature is perceived at a given moment.

Aggregating at the level of entities: entity_network()

You may want to link authors, institutions or journals rather than documents. This is not a different kind of network, nor a different measure: it is the same coupling (or co-citation), computed for entities that aggregate documents. An entity publishes several documents and can cite the same reference several times. entity_network() takes this into account: for each reference shared by two entities, it counts the minimum number of times the two entities cite it (Zhao and Strotmann 2008). If one author cites a reference in two of their articles and another in three, the reference counts for two.

The consequence is that a reference that two entities cite repeatedly contributes more to the tie than a reference each of them cites once. With the coupling strength, the weight is

w_{AB} = \frac{1}{L(A) \, L(B)} \sum_{j} \min(C_{Aj}, C_{Bj}) \, \log\left(\frac{N}{f_j}\right)

where C_{Aj} and C_{Bj} are the numbers of times A and B cite the reference j, L(A) is the total number of citations made by A, N the number of citing documents and f_j the number of documents citing j. The method argument accepts the same methods as biblio_coupling() ("angle", "strength", "similarity", "jaccard" and "vladutz"), each adapted with the minimum rule (see ?entity_network for the formulas), and the network argument chooses between "coupling" (entities that cite the same references) and "cocitation" (entities whose references are cited together, as in author co-citation analysis).

The input needs one row per citation and per entity: we merge the table of direct citations with the table of authors. A document with several authors appears several times, hence allow.cartesian = TRUE.

entity_citations <- merge(Ref_stagflation,
                          Authors_stagflation,
                          by.x = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                          by.y = "ItemID_Ref",
                          allow.cartesian = TRUE)

entity_network(entity_citations,
               source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
               ref = "ItemID_Ref",
               entity = "Author.y",
               method = "angle")
#>             from         to      weight     Source     Target Weighting_method
#>           <char>     <char>       <num>     <char>     <char>           <char>
#>    1: ALBANESI-S     BALL-L 0.048592953 ALBANESI-S     BALL-L            angle
#>    2: ALBANESI-S   BARSKY-R 0.063021872 ALBANESI-S   BARSKY-R            angle
#>    3: ALBANESI-S    BEYER-A 0.034585723 ALBANESI-S    BEYER-A            angle
#>    4: ALBANESI-S BILBIIE-FO 0.064282435 ALBANESI-S BILBIIE-FO            angle
#>    5: ALBANESI-S    BORDO-M 0.043519414 ALBANESI-S    BORDO-M            angle
#>   ---
#> 3461: WILLIAMS-J WILLIAMS-N 0.028213825 WILLIAMS-J WILLIAMS-N            angle
#> 3462: WILLIAMS-J    YOUNG-W 0.008748736 WILLIAMS-J    YOUNG-W            angle
#> 3463: WILLIAMS-J      ZHA-T 0.028213825 WILLIAMS-J      ZHA-T            angle
#> 3464: WILLIAMS-N      ZHA-T 1.000000000 WILLIAMS-N      ZHA-T            angle
#> 3465: WOODFORD-M    YOUNG-W 0.020672456 WOODFORD-M    YOUNG-W            angle

For a co-citation network of entities, the entity column must describe the cited reference (the author or the journal of the cited document) rather than the citing one. Here, the journals of the cited documents:

entity_network(Ref_stagflation,
                    source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                    ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                    entity = "Journal",
                    network = "cocitation",
                    weight_threshold = 3)
#> Warning: Dropping 738 rows with a missing identifier.

Co-authorship: coauth_network()

Co-authorship links the authors (or institutions, or countries) who sign documents together. You could build it with biblio_coupling(), authors being the source and documents the ref, but coupling is not designed for it: what matters here is how to count a collaboration. coauth_network() offers three ways, and an optional normalisation by the productivity of the authors.

To see what they do, take a toy example: three authors, a, b and c, sign document 1; a and b sign document 2.

toy <- data.frame(author = c("a", "b", "c", "a", "b"),
                  paper  = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2))

Full counting ("full_counting") gives one point to each pair of authors for each document they co-sign. The weight is the number of co-signed documents. Here a–b gets 2 points, and a–c and b–c one point each. The problem is that big collaborations weigh more: a document with ten authors creates 45 pairs, so it adds 45 points to the network, whereas a document with two authors adds one.

coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper", method = "full_counting")
#>      from     to weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>  <num> <char> <char>
#> 1:      b      a      2      b      a
#> 2:      c      a      1      c      a
#> 3:      c      b      1      c      b

Fractional counting ("fractional_counting") shares the value of a document among the co-authors, so that a large collaboration does not dominate (Perianes-Rodriguez, Waltman, and Van Eck 2016). A document with n authors gives 1/(n-1) to each pair of its authors, so that the weights of all the ties of an author in this document sum to one: each author “spends” one unit of collaboration per document, split among the co-authors. In the toy example, document 1 has three authors, so each of its three pairs receives 1/2; document 2 has two authors, so a–b receives 1. The weight of a–b is 1/2 + 1 = 1.5, and that of a–c and b–c is 1/2: the pair that collaborated in a small team is worth more than a pair in a large team. Perianes-Rodriguez, Waltman, and Van Eck (2016) compare full and fractional counting on bibliometric networks, and show that the choice changes the picture.

coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper", method = "fractional_counting")
#>      from     to weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>  <num> <char> <char>
#> 1:      b      a    1.5      b      a
#> 2:      c      a    0.5      c      a
#> 3:      c      b    0.5      c      b

Refined fractional counting ("fractional_counting_refined"), inspired by Leydesdorff and Park (2017-02), goes one step further: each document, rather than each author, has a total weight of one in the network. A document with n authors creates n(n-1)/2 pairs, so each pair gets 2/(n(n-1)). Document 1 gives 1/3 to each of its three pairs (3 \times 1/3 = 1) and document 2 gives 1 to a–b. The weight of a–b is 1/3 + 1 \approx 1.33. The sum of all the weights of the network is then the number of co-authored documents.

coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper", method = "fractional_counting_refined")
#>      from     to    weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>     <num> <char> <char>
#> 1:      b      a 1.3333333      b      a
#> 2:      c      a 0.3333333      c      a
#> 3:      c      b 0.3333333      c      b

In all cases, documents with a single author are ignored, since they create no tie.

Normalising by productivity. Prolific authors have many collaborations simply because they publish a lot. With cosine_normalized = TRUE, the weight is divided by \sqrt{P_i P_j}, where P_i is the number of co-authored documents of author i (Salton’s cosine, as for the coupling angle). The weight then measures whether two authors collaborate a lot relative to how much each of them collaborates in general. In the toy example, P_a = P_b = 2 and P_c = 1: with full counting, a–b gets 2/\sqrt{2 \times 2} = 1 and a–c gets 1/\sqrt{2 \times 1} \approx 0.71.

coauth_network(toy, authors = "author", articles = "paper",
               method = "full_counting", cosine_normalized = TRUE)
#>      from     to    weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>     <num> <char> <char>
#> 1:      b      a 1.0000000      b      a
#> 2:      c      a 0.7071068      c      a
#> 3:      c      b 0.7071068      c      b

On the stagflation authors, with fractional counting and the cosine normalisation:

coauth_network(Authors_stagflation,
               authors = "Author",
               articles = "ItemID_Ref",
               method = "fractional_counting",
               cosine_normalized = TRUE)
#>              from            to    weight        Source        Target
#>            <char>        <char>     <num>        <char>        <char>
#>  1:       CHARI-V    ALBANESI-S 0.3535534       CHARI-V    ALBANESI-S
#>  2:  CHRISTIANO-L    ALBANESI-S 0.2500000  CHRISTIANO-L    ALBANESI-S
#>  3:  CHRISTIANO-L       CHARI-V 0.3535534  CHRISTIANO-L       CHARI-V
#>  4:   CUKIERMAN-A     BRUNNER-K 0.3535534   CUKIERMAN-A     BRUNNER-K
#>  5:  EICHENBAUM-M       CHARI-V 0.3535534  EICHENBAUM-M       CHARI-V
#>  6:  EICHENBAUM-M  CHRISTIANO-L 0.2500000  EICHENBAUM-M  CHRISTIANO-L
#>  7: EICHENGREEN-B       BORDO-M 1.0000000 EICHENGREEN-B       BORDO-M
#>  8:      EUSEPI-S     BULLARD-J 1.0000000      EUSEPI-S     BULLARD-J
#>  9:      FARMER-R       BEYER-A 1.0000000      FARMER-R       BEYER-A
#> 10:  FITZGERALD-T  CHRISTIANO-L 0.5000000  FITZGERALD-T  CHRISTIANO-L
#> 11:        GALI-J   BLANCHARD-O 0.7071068        GALI-J   BLANCHARD-O
#> 12:        GALI-J     CLARIDA-R 0.3535534        GALI-J     CLARIDA-R

Note that, for historical reasons, coauth_network() orients its edges with Source > Target, the opposite of the other functions.

Filtering the edges: thresholds and backbones

A bibliometric network built from a large corpus is often too dense to be read or clustered: almost every pair of documents shares at least one reference. There are two ways of simplifying it.

  • A threshold, as seen above: weight_threshold keeps the pairs sharing at least k references. It is simple and fast, but arbitrary, and it is global: the same threshold applies to a document with a hundred references and to a document with five.
  • A backbone: keep only the ties that are statistically unlikely under a null model, that is, the ties that are stronger than what the position of the nodes in the network would produce by chance. This is the aim of the backbone package (Neal 2026), which is complementary to biblionetwork: biblionetwork computes the edges and their weights, backbone decides which ones are worth keeping.

backbone offers two families of methods, and they do not start from the same object.

Filters of weighted networks (backbone_from_weighted(), with the disparity filter of Serrano, Boguñá, and Vespignani (2009) for instance) start from a weighted one-mode network. They can be run directly on the edges produced by biblionetwork: convert the edge list into a graph and give it to backbone. Since these filters assume that the weights are strengths of ties, it is more natural to feed them with the number of shared references (normalized_weight_only = FALSE) than with a cosine.

edges <- biblio_coupling(Ref_stagflation,
                         source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                         ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                         normalized_weight_only = FALSE,
                         weight_threshold = 2)

# The weighted graph; the number of shared references is the weight
graph <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  edges[, .(from, to, weight = nb_shared_references)],
  directed = FALSE
)

# The disparity filter: keep an edge if its weight is significantly high
# compared to the other edges of (at least one of) its two nodes
backbone <- backbone::backbone_from_weighted(graph, model = "disparity", alpha = 0.05)
c(edges_before = igraph::ecount(graph), edges_after = igraph::ecount(backbone))
#> edges_before  edges_after
#>         1501           16

Filters of bipartite projections (backbone_from_projection(), with models such as "sdsm", the stochastic degree sequence model) do not start from the edges but from the original two-mode table: they compare the number of references that two documents share with the number expected if documents cited references at random, given how many references each document cites and how many documents cite each reference. The input is the table of citations as an incidence matrix (documents in rows, references in columns), which is the same table as the one you give to biblionetwork.

# Incidence matrix of the citations: 1 if the document (row) cites the reference (column)
incidence <- unclass(table(Ref_stagflation$Citing_ItemID_Ref, Ref_stagflation$ItemID_Ref))
incidence[incidence > 1] <- 1

# Statistically significant coupling ties (the filter is applied to the rows)
backbone_sdsm <- backbone::backbone_from_projection(incidence, model = "sdsm", alpha = 0.05)
sum(backbone_sdsm) / 2   # number of ties kept (the matrix is symmetric)
#> [1] 553

Two practical remarks.

  • The statistical models test the count of shared references, not a normalised weight. Run them on the full table, without a weight_threshold: a pair removed by the threshold cannot be tested. The backbone then replaces the threshold. You can use biblionetwork afterwards, on the pairs kept, if you want the normalised weights of the surviving ties (merge the two edge lists by pair of documents).
  • These tests are computationally heavier than the edge computation of biblionetwork, and the null models are not designed for the huge corpora that biblionetwork handles: on a large corpus, split it by time window, or start from the filters of weighted networks.

networkflow integrates both steps: its function build_dynamic_networks() can compute the coupling edges and apply a statistical backbone for each time window (see the networkflow documentation).

Beyond bibliometrics

Nothing in the functions of biblionetwork is specific to bibliography. They take a table with two columns, “a source that is linked to a ref”, and build the network of the sources that share refs (coupling) or of the refs that share sources (co-citation). The words “document” and “reference” are only the vocabulary of the field in which the package was written. Whenever you have a two-mode relation, the same questions can be asked:

Networks of accounts on a social media platform

Take a table of the accounts of a social media platform and the accounts they follow. Two accounts that follow many of the same accounts probably listen to the same voices: this is the bibliographic coupling of the “follows” (the account is the “document”, the accounts it follows are its “bibliography”). In the same way, two accounts that repost the same posts are close in what they amplify. The following table is invented, for the sake of the example.

follows <- data.table(
  account = c("ann", "ann", "ann", "ben", "ben", "ben", "cleo", "cleo", "dan", "dan", "eve", "eve", "eve"),
  follows = c("news_desk", "dev_tools", "open_web", "news_desk", "dev_tools", "open_web",
              "news_desk", "celebrity", "celebrity", "news_desk", "celebrity", "dev_tools", "open_web")
)

# Accounts close because they follow the same accounts
biblio_coupling(follows, source = "account", ref = "follows", normalized_weight_only = FALSE)
#>       from     to    weight nb_shared_references Source Target
#>     <char> <char>     <num>                <int> <char> <char>
#>  1:    ann    ben 1.0000000                    3    ann    ben
#>  2:    ann   cleo 0.4082483                    1    ann   cleo
#>  3:    ben   cleo 0.4082483                    1    ben   cleo
#>  4:    ann    dan 0.4082483                    1    ann    dan
#>  5:    ben    dan 0.4082483                    1    ben    dan
#>  6:   cleo    dan 1.0000000                    2   cleo    dan
#>  7:    ann    eve 0.6666667                    2    ann    eve
#>  8:    ben    eve 0.6666667                    2    ben    eve
#>  9:   cleo    eve 0.4082483                    1   cleo    eve
#> 10:    dan    eve 0.4082483                    1    dan    eve

Here news_desk and celebrity are followed by almost everybody: following them says little. The idf-based methods, designed for the “classics” of a bibliography, are exactly what is needed to discount the accounts followed by a large audience:

biblio_coupling(follows, source = "account", ref = "follows", method = "strength")
#>       from     to     weight Source Target
#>     <char> <char>      <num> <char> <char>
#>  1:    ann    ben 0.13831053    ann    ben
#>  2:    ann   cleo 0.03719059    ann   cleo
#>  3:    ben   cleo 0.03719059    ben   cleo
#>  4:    ann    dan 0.03719059    ann    dan
#>  5:    ben    dan 0.03719059    ben    dan
#>  6:   cleo    dan 0.18349229   cleo    dan
#>  7:    ann    eve 0.11351681    ann    eve
#>  8:    ben    eve 0.11351681    ben    eve
#>  9:   cleo    eve 0.08513760   cleo    eve
#> 10:    dan    eve 0.08513760    dan    eve

This is how coupling is used on social media data: popular targets (an account followed by millions) are the equivalent of the classics of a field, and the warning on memory of Section 2 matters even more, as such targets are much more frequent than in a bibliography. Reposts work the same way, with source the account and ref the reposted post. And co-citation answers the mirror question: which posts are reposted by the same accounts?

reposts <- data.table(
  account = c("ann", "ann", "ben", "ben", "cleo", "cleo", "dan"),
  post    = c("p1", "p2", "p1", "p2", "p2", "p3", "p3")
)
biblio_cocitation(reposts, source = "account", ref = "post")
#>      from     to    weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>     <num> <char> <char>
#> 1:     p1     p2 0.8164966     p1     p2
#> 2:     p2     p3 0.4082483     p2     p3

Because a network of this kind is often dense (and the measures do not tell which ties are “surprising”), the backbone of Section 6 is particularly useful there.

Networks of words

A text is a “document” that “cites” words. The coupling of texts links the texts that use the same words; the co-citation of words links the words that appear together. We illustrate it with the titles of the stagflation documents.

titles <- Nodes_stagflation[!is.na(Title), .(ItemID_Ref, Title)]

# One row per title and distinct word. Short words and a few stop words are dropped:
# like popular references, very frequent words create a huge number of pairs and carry little meaning.
stop_words <- c("the", "and", "for", "with", "from", "that", "this", "its", "are", "was",
                "into", "their", "between", "some", "what", "how", "when", "than", "have", "new")
words <- titles[, .(word = unique(tolower(unlist(strsplit(Title, "[^A-Za-z]+"))))), by = ItemID_Ref]
words <- words[nchar(word) > 3 & !word %in% stop_words]
words[1:5]
#>    ItemID_Ref      word
#>        <char>    <char>
#> 1:  112854189   richard
#> 2:  112854189     nixon
#> 3:  112854189 pressured
#> 4:  112854189    arthur
#> 5:  112854189     burns

Titles are coupled when they share words. The coupling strength gives more weight to rare words than to words such as “inflation” or “policy”, present in many titles:

title_edges <- biblio_coupling(words, source = "ItemID_Ref", ref = "word",
                               method = "strength", normalized_weight_only = FALSE,
                               weight_threshold = 2)
title_edges[order(-weight)][1:5]
#>          from       to   weight nb_shared_references     Source   Target
#>        <char>   <char>    <num>                <int>     <char>   <char>
#> 1:   15862899   804985 2.172583                    2   15862899   804985
#> 2:  105203318   927924 1.563913                    2  105203318   927924
#> 3: 1111111190 49791437 1.376890                    2 1111111190 49791437
#> 4:   37660505  6071710 1.376890                    2   37660505  6071710
#> 5:   37799073 44208484 1.350867                    3   37799073 44208484

Words are linked when they appear in the same titles (this is the co-citation of words). The words that always appear together are the fixed expressions of the corpus:

word_edges <- biblio_cocitation(words, source = "ItemID_Ref", ref = "word",
                                weight_threshold = 2, normalized_weight_only = FALSE)
word_edges[order(-nb_shared_citations)][1:8, .(from, to, weight, nb_shared_citations)]
#>         from        to    weight nb_shared_citations
#>       <char>    <char>     <num>               <int>
#> 1:  monetary    policy 0.7441311                  97
#> 2:     great inflation 0.3400046                  23
#> 3: inflation    policy 0.1533110                  22
#> 4:    states    united 0.9770084                  21
#> 5:    policy     rules 0.3127716                  18
#> 6: inflation  monetary 0.1154735                  15
#> 7:  monetary     rules 0.2687343                  14
#> 8:     price    shocks 0.3614784                  14

The same logic applies to any “bag of …” representation (n-grams, keywords, hashtags, named entities, topics of a topic model…). For the words in the titles of references, coupling_descriptive() implements a more elaborate approach (Liu 2017), which couples documents that cite different but related references.

What to check before using it outside bibliometrics

  • Orientation. source is the node of the network produced by biblio_coupling(); ref is what the nodes share. If the network you obtain has the wrong nodes, you probably swapped the columns (the function warns you when no pair is found).
  • Popular targets. A target shared by very many sources (a celebrity, a stop word) creates a quadratic number of pairs and carries little information. Remove it, or use a method that discounts it, or work by time window.
  • The meaning of “length”. The normalisation by the length of the bibliography assumes that having many refs is a form of dilution. For an account following 10,000 accounts, this is reasonable; for a text, the length of the document in words may be a different matter.
  • Time. Coupling ties are fixed when the source is created. For social media data, the “follows” are not dated in the same way as references: think about the moment at which the table is observed.

A last word on choosing

All the functions return undirected edges (one row per pair), never modify the table you give them, and return an empty table, with a warning that says why, when no pair of nodes is linked.
